title: Issue 1 Cover — Released Canon
summary: Released canonical cover. The selling image is the absurdly ordinary collision between armed-looking 9th-century Norse adults and a municipal waiting room: temporal displacement has become somebody's caseload. This unit exists to expose the released cover as the chef-facing trade-dress authority; do not redesign it.
settingText: Municipal Department of Temporal Integration waiting room, fluorescent present-day New York civic interior.
panelPlan: REFERENCE-LOCKED COVER. Pixel-read production/references/vikings-2026/assets/covers/issue-01-cover-trade-dress.jpg and preserve it as canon rather than creating a new concept. The local file is an exact byte-for-byte copy of the released StarSplitterVisions Issue 1 cover.

The canonical composition uses a large white trade-dress masthead above the art. Below it, Carrie and two Norse men sit frontally in an ordinary municipal waiting room under a digital Now Serving display; the visual joke comes from bureaucratic normalcy surrounding visibly displaced people, not from caricature.

The seated central mass must read instantly: Carrie with clipboard/coffee at left, the serious Norse figures centered/right, mundane waiting-room chairs, fluorescent ceiling, other ordinary patrons behind them.

If a reconstruction is ever explicitly requested, match the existing cover's composition, character identities, typography, painted rendering, and publication design as closely as possible. Do not 'improve' or modernize the design.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR — RELEASED CANON ESSENCE: ordinary waiting-room patrons and municipal staff share the room with visibly displaced Norse adults and continue their own business. Preserve the deadpan social temperature: waiting, reading, watching the number display, drinking coffee, doing desk work. Nobody gathers, points, photographs them, or turns the room into a spectacle.

directionInline.text: RELEASE LOCK: The canonical asset already exists in StarSplitterVisions and is the source of truth. Use the existing released asset for publication. Generate a replacement only if the user explicitly reopens the released cover.

title: Issue 2 Cover — Landfall Bushwick
summary: Sell the issue through one contradiction: the city has given six people a legal address, but a fifth-floor room and one brass key have not yet become home. The image should make shelter feel concrete, cramped, provisional, and worth climbing toward.
settingText: Narrow Bushwick apartment stairwell rising toward the fifth-floor landing and apartment 5B at night.
panelPlan: Single dominant vertical image: look upward through the cramped stairwell toward Carrie at the fifth-floor landing, where the ordinary apartment door and one brass key are the visual destination.

Carrie is higher in frame with the key catching a small practical highlight; the household climbs below with bundles and gear, compressed by the stair geometry. Bjorn studies the door/landing as shelter to be evaluated, not as a gift to celebrate.

The cover should feel physically tiring and enticing: repeating flights, old paint, practical light fixtures, railings, brick/plaster, glimpses of fire-escape geometry. The building is ordinary Brooklyn, not gothic or threatening.
Focal hierarchy at thumbnail: bright key/door destination first, upward-moving household silhouette second, deep stairwell third. Do not distribute equal emphasis across all six faces.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: include one ordinary building resident moving through the cramped stairwell on an unrelated errand—laundry basket, grocery bag, keys, trash or mail. They simply negotiate the narrow space and continue past the household. Their posture should say 'people are moving in' rather than 'Vikings are here.' Keep this resident small and secondary.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: make the historical household materially obvious against the ordinary building—established Norse clothing, bundled possessions and alert physical caution against painted railings, apartment doors, electrical fixtures and hallway light. Do not modernize their silhouettes to make them blend.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the apartment already settled, the witnessed thumbprint, the key handoff payoff, the neighbor reciprocity, or later domestic warmth.

directionInline.text: Palette beneath masthead: cool nocturnal stairwell neutrals with localized warm apartment/building light; avoid sepia nostalgia.
The ordinary resident must not become a reaction gag. A brief glance or practical step-aside is acceptable; staring, smiling at the spectacle, photographing them, or stopping the stairwell is not.

title: Issue 3 Cover — Territory
summary: Sell Gunnar's need for one fixed point in a city whose scale and systems remain unfamiliar. The irresistible image is not a rooftop adventure; it is a competent navigator discovering that before anything else he needs north.
settingText: Bushwick apartment rooftop at dawn with the Manhattan/Brooklyn urban horizon and street grid beyond.
panelPlan: Single iconic rooftop image. Gunnar stands near the parapet at dawn, small but visually decisive against a huge city. His attention is on sun, shadow, avenue alignment and horizon rather than on a device.

Use roof lines, parapet, water towers, antennae and the receding street grid to create a powerful directional composition that naturally points through the city. The image should make 'north' feel like a physical problem the reader can almost solve with him.
Keep Gunnar grounded and practical: no mystical pose, no glowing compass effect, no fantasy map overlay. His body language is intent observation.
Focal hierarchy at thumbnail: Gunnar's clear silhouette against morning sky first; one strong directional line through the city second; rooftop texture third.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: on a neighboring roof or distant fire escape, include one tiny New Yorker doing a mundane dawn task—coffee, laundry, watering a plant, taking out a bag or checking a phone—without looking toward Gunnar. The figure is environmental life, not a secondary character.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: Gunnar should look like a ninth-century navigator using sun, shadow and urban geometry to solve a real problem while the surrounding rooftops treat dawn as the beginning of an ordinary workday.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show Silas, the phone compass, rooftop metal, hearth construction, fire, or the later ownership/winter dispute.

directionInline.text: Use crisp early-morning blues/greens/brick tones and actual urban color; the roof should feel lived-in and real, not apocalyptic.
Do not turn the roof into a heroic overlook or mystical revelation. The visual pleasure is a serious historical navigator solving north inside a city that does not know it has become his instrument.

title: Issue 4 Cover — The Iron Worm
summary: Sell the subway as a perfectly ordinary New York system that feels like an outrageous proposition to people who have never accepted the premise of a road beneath the city.
settingText: New York City subway platform and arriving train, practical fluorescent underground environment.
panelPlan: Single dynamic but grounded platform composition. A subway train enters or rushes along the platform, its stainless-steel mass and lit windows forming the dominant 'iron worm' shape without literally turning it into a creature.

Carrie stands within normal commuter behavior, already oriented to boarding. Bjorn and Gunnar remain near her but visibly assess the train/tunnel as infrastructure they have not yet agreed is sensible.
Use tunnel perspective, platform edge, tile, fluorescent strips and train motion to create strong depth and energy. Ordinary commuters should barely react to either the train or the Vikings.
Thumbnail hierarchy: bright train front/windows and tunnel vanishing point first, three-character silhouette group second. Avoid a busy crowd where the hook disappears.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: commuters pass within arm's reach of Bjorn and Gunnar while checking phones, adjusting headphones, reading the platform display, lining up at doors or entering the train. Nobody stops, points, photographs them, recoils, gives them ceremonial space or turns the platform into a reaction shot.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: Bjorn and Gunnar's established period clothing, stance and wary spacing should contrast sharply with stainless steel, yellow platform edge, tiled walls, fluorescent light and the mass of the arriving train. Carrie is physically inside the commuter flow; they are not yet.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the later annex, hidden staff route, transfer solution, getting home, or Gunnar's return achievement.

directionInline.text: Do not literalize the title with monster imagery, scales, eyes, teeth, smoke, or fantasy symbolism. The joke is that the real subway is strange enough.

The background comedy is total procedural normalcy: the train arrives, doors open, people board, and New York remains more interested in getting somewhere than in the two ninth-century men evaluating the entire premise.

title: Issue 5 Cover — The Neighborhood
summary: Sell the moment when a vast anonymous city starts becoming a collection of repeated human encounters. The cover should make an ordinary morning coffee line feel like the beginning of being known.
settingText: Bushwick sidewalk coffee cart on a busy but recognizable morning block.
panelPlan: Single street-corner image centered on Bjorn at a coffee cart within the morning line. Gunnar is nearby; the vendor works normally; commuters move around them with practiced rhythm.
Give Bjorn an over-sweet first coffee or a skeptical reaction to it as the specific visual comedy. The humor is personal and modest, not broad slapstick.
Let the block itself support the premise through recurring visual anchors—awning edges, stoops, cart steam, storefront geometry—but do not turn the cover into a montage of every neighborhood subplot.
Thumbnail hierarchy: Bjorn and the bright steaming cup first, cart silhouette second, recognizable block rhythm third. The reader should feel 'same place, tomorrow.'

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: the vendor treats Bjorn as a customer, not a curiosity. The person behind him checks a phone, studies the cart menu or watches the line advance; pedestrians continue past with work bags, earbuds, dogs or delivery gear. Nobody is visibly entertained by Bjorn's clothing or by his reaction to the coffee.
DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: keep Bjorn's established historical clothing, physical gravity and diplomatic seriousness fully intact while every other visual cue says ordinary weekday coffee transaction.

Spoiler ceiling: do not show the vendor remembering his corrected order, Sal's named relationship with Gunnar, the carved token, laundry familiarity, neighbor snack reciprocity, or the issue's recognition payoff.

directionInline.text: Use lively morning city color and steam; avoid making the neighborhood quaint, nostalgic, or sanitized.
Stage this as a real New York coffee line that has absorbed a Viking without changing its rhythm.

title: Issue 6 Cover — The Tally of Dishonor
summary: Sell Bjorn's confrontation with money that exists mainly as institutional record. The visual contradiction is a transparent bank full of desks, screens and ordinary customers but no visible hoard.
settingText: Glass-front neighborhood bank on a Bushwick commercial block, daytime.
panelPlan: Single cover image from just outside or at the threshold of a glass-front bank. Bjorn dominates the foreground, studying the transparent facade as if the building has failed to contain the treasure it claims to manage.

Through the glass: mundane service desks, queue ropes, screens, customers and tellers. In the glass reflections: ordinary neighborhood commerce—coffee, groceries, buses—quietly showing what abstract money actually touches.
Carrie can be slightly ahead toward the appointment; Gunnar studies the system. Keep Bjorn dignified and genuinely analytical, not baffled slapstick.
Thumbnail hierarchy: Bjorn's large silhouette against a clean glass rectangle first; sterile bank interior second; reflected street life third.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: inside the bank, customers fill forms, wait in queue, speak with tellers or walk out with receipts. A guard or employee may acknowledge Bjorn only at the practical level required to manage the line or door. Nobody stares at his clothes and no security response occurs merely because he looks historical.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: Bjorn's established Norse appearance should be unmistakable against clean glass, queue stanchions, screens and service desks. Everyone around him already accepts that numbers on screens represent money; he is the only person in frame treating that premise as an unresolved material question.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show successful account approval, debit card, household shopping, toaster, debt ledger, or Bjorn's final acceptance of planned debt.

directionInline.text: Use clear glass/cool institutional light contrasted with normal street color. No piles of coins, treasure chests, fantasy gold, or metaphorical money rain.
Do not sell the scene as novelty—'Viking enters bank.' Sell Bjorn's serious conflict with invisible value while the institution continues processing customers as usual.

title: Issue 7 Cover — The Skaldic Interface
summary: Sell the library as the city's enormous external memory: Gunnar wants context older than yesterday, and New York keeps more recorded voices than any household could carry.
settingText: Neighborhood public library stacks and reading room, daytime.
panelPlan: Single deep-perspective library image. Gunnar stands at the threshold of a long aisle or reading-room opening, visually pulled into rows of accumulated books that recede far beyond what one household could remember.

Bjorn is secondary, present as another displaced reader rather than as the carrier of a later gag. A rolling cart or nearby shelf may contain history volumes, but no particular book or factual dispute should be called out.
Keep the public library ordinary, used and civic—fluorescent/daylit, carts, tables, patrons—not a magical archive or cathedral of knowledge.
Thumbnail hierarchy: Gunnar framed by powerful shelf geometry first; deep accumulation of books second; ordinary civic patrons third.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: library patrons keep reading, browsing shelves, using computers, supervising a child, shelving books or pushing a cart. A librarian may cross the composition without treating Gunnar or Bjorn as an attraction. Their historical appearance is visually conspicuous; socially, the room stays quiet and routine.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: Gunnar's reaction should be to the physical scale of stored memory, not to people noticing him. The other patrons' calm use of the same shelves makes the proposition stranger and larger.

Spoiler ceiling: do not reveal the inaccurate Viking-history book, Bjorn's complaint, written corrections, why the library keeps disputed material, borrowing resolution, or the final shared-reading payoff.

directionInline.text: Avoid glowing books, holograms, mystical runes, or fantasy-library imagery. The real visual abundance is enough.
No patron-reaction gag. The public library's indifference is part of the scale: this impossible abundance of recorded memory is ordinary civic infrastructure to everyone else.

title: Issue 8 Cover — Provision
summary: Sell the seasonal mismatch: New York sees a pleasant April day; Bjorn and Gunnar see the beginning of winter preparation. The cover should make competence look urgent before any crisis exists.
settingText: Bushwick bus stop beside a small green public park on a mild April morning.
panelPlan: Single spring-morning image at a bus stop beside a modest public green space. Budding trees, damp pavement and soft light make the season unmistakably pleasant.

Carrie waits like an ordinary commuter. Bjorn and Gunnar, beside her, study the available ground, sky, grocery bag and new growth with practical winter-provision attention. Their seriousness should be funny only because the day is so mild.
Use the park rectangle and bus-shelter geometry to make the unused land visually tempting without showing anyone planting or claiming it.
Thumbnail hierarchy: three figures against bright spring green first; the small field-like patch of public land second; weather-rich sky third.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: populate the bus stop and sidewalk sparingly with routine spring behavior—someone scrolling a phone, sipping coffee, carrying a tote, walking a dog or checking the arrival sign. Nobody shares Bjorn and Gunnar's winter urgency, and nobody reacts to their historical clothing.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: Carrie waits like a commuter. Bjorn and Gunnar visually inventory sky, soil, growth and available land as practical seasonal data. The same mild morning means entirely different things to them.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the planting proposal, community-garden alternative, later storm preparation, weather alert, storm arrival, or the fact that preparation succeeds.

directionInline.text: Use genuinely fresh spring greens and cool wet-city color. Do not visually foreshadow winter with snow, split-season effects, ominous storm clouds, or fantasy prophecy.
Do not make New Yorkers smirk at the Vikings. Their lack of interest is the joke; they simply interpret April as April.

title: Issue 9 Cover — Trial of Toil
summary: Sell Bjorn's most difficult practical problem: modern safety and shared competence have removed many of the jobs that once proved his worth. The image is a formidable capable man with nothing urgent to do.
settingText: Apartment 5B during an already-functioning morning routine.
panelPlan: Single quiet interior image. Bjorn sits or stands near the table in the foreground with his large capable hands empty; a prepared mug of coffee waits for him.
Behind and around him, Gunnar and the two male Kin are already absorbed in ordinary useful routines—breakfast, laundry, household preparation—without looking to Bjorn for direction.
The emotional contradiction must read immediately: nothing is wrong, everyone is competent, and that is exactly what has unsettled him. Do not make him pathetic, sulking, or theatrically isolated.
Thumbnail hierarchy: Bjorn's empty hands/solid silhouette first; visible activity flowing around him second; safe lived-in apartment third.

CITY-CONTINUES DETAIL: through the apartment window or a narrow exterior glimpse, show ordinary morning movement continuing outside—delivery bike, bus, pedestrians, neighboring windows—without creating a second focal scene. The city is functioning; Bjorn's deeper problem is that increasingly, so is the household.
Spoiler ceiling: do not show the power-strip incident, bodega labor attempt, support group, stair catch, later admission about protection, or the behavioral resolution.

directionInline.text: Let ordinary daylight and household color carry the scene. No battle imagery, symbolic chains, broken weapons, or melodramatic darkness.
This is the private-space version of New York indifference: nobody is rejecting Bjorn or reacting to him. The world simply no longer requires his intervention every minute.

title: Issue 10 Cover — Belonging
summary: Sell successful integration as a loss of central control: the household now has separate mornings, separate routes and places Carrie did not assign. The cover should make independence look ordinary and slightly startling.
settingText: Apartment 5B doorway, building stairwell and Bushwick sidewalk during the morning departure.
panelPlan: Single composition built around branching movement rather than a lineup. Use the apartment doorway, stair flight, building entrance and sidewalk to create several natural paths through one image.

Carrie arrives with her familiar folder near the compositional center while household members are already leaving in different directions for ordinary plans. Nobody is running away, arguing, or seeking permission.
Bjorn should participate in the normal movement rather than command it. The strongest idea is that the household reconverges because people choose to, not because Carrie or Bjorn schedules them.
Thumbnail hierarchy: Carrie's stationary folder-bearing figure against several clear diverging silhouettes first; doorway/street branching geometry second. Keep faces secondary to movement.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: neighbors, commuters or delivery workers move through the stairwell and sidewalk around the household's branching departures without stopping to watch. They may hold a door, step around a bundle, pass on the stairs or continue toward work with ordinary urban courtesy and indifference.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: keep the household's historical clothing visibly distinct inside otherwise routine morning circulation. The building and block should behave as though these people are now part of the neighborhood's normal visual field.
Spoiler ceiling: do not reveal the specific destinations, garbage-night salvage, sanitation-worker authority, carved object, return order, or Carrie's end-of-issue conclusion.

directionInline.text: Use normal morning color and motion. Do not add literal arrows, maps, diagrams, or symbolic path graphics.
By this issue, the city not reacting carries meaning: their visible difference has not disappeared, but routine has made it socially ordinary.

title: Issue 11 Cover — War Council
summary: Sell the problem of preparing for judgment without manufacturing one collective answer. The household shares a table and a home, but the city is about to ask five adults what each one wants.
settingText: Apartment 5B table at night with an official review notice and ordinary household objects.
panelPlan: Single near-overhead/table composition. An official review notice is the small sharp center of the image, but the visual field around it belongs to five different adults rather than one collective war council.

Arrange distinct hands, seated positions and ordinary personal/household objects around the table—key, closed book, mug, laundry/fabric, practical tools—without turning the objects into a forensic evidence display.
Carrie's folder may sit at one edge, visibly smaller than the lived life around it. Bjorn should not occupy a throne-like head position; preserve the issue's pressure around separate answers.
Thumbnail hierarchy: pale official notice at center first; five distinct human positions/hands around it second; lived-in apartment texture third. The top-down geometry should be bold and clean.

INSTITUTIONAL-INDIFFERENCE DETAIL: make the official review notice visually dull—plain paper, practical case typography, ordinary municipal formatting. No red warning stamp, ominous seal, black envelope, thriller lighting or visual villainy. The pressure comes from what completely routine paperwork can require of five adults.

CITY-CONTINUES DETAIL: if an exterior sliver is visible through a window or doorway, keep ordinary building life moving faintly beyond the table. Do not invent spectators; this cover's indifference is bureaucratic rather than public.
Spoiler ceiling: do not reveal anyone's specific future answer, Silas's bounded help, the no-rehearsal conclusion, hearing procedure, or any evidence/result from Issue 12.

directionInline.text: The title is intentionally grander than the room. Do not add weapons, battle maps, tactical holograms, or medieval council staging.
The document should look boring enough to be ignored on any other day. That is what makes its power over the household unsettling.

title: Issue 12 Cover — Permanent Residency / Trial by Combat
summary: Sell the season finale through the cleanest collision in the series: Bjorn arrives for a municipal status hearing wearing armor, while five adults are about to find out whether the city's record can describe the lives they have actually built.
settingText: Municipal hearing-center security checkpoint and corridor, morning.
panelPlan: Single iconic finale image. Bjorn, weaponless but wearing his established armor, stands inside or immediately before a mundane municipal metal-detector/security arch. Carrie holds a folder; the other four adults wait as separate people rather than a retinue.

Use the security arch and fluorescent corridor like a ceremonial gate without making the building grand. A bored/competent security context should make Bjorn's armor visually outrageous and institutionally routine at the same time.
Keep all weapons absent. The tension comes from judgment, classification and self-definition, not physical danger. Bjorn's body language is composed and serious, not aggressive.
Thumbnail hierarchy: armored Bjorn framed by the detector arch first; folder and separate applicant silhouettes second; plain hearing-center corridor third.

BACKGROUND BEHAVIOR: security staff behave like professionals solving an ordinary checkpoint problem. One officer may gesture toward a tray, wand, belt procedure or next position with no theatrical surprise. Other visitors wait their turn, remove metal objects, look at paperwork or stare ahead; nobody gathers around Bjorn's armor.

DISPLACEMENT DETAIL: maximize the visual contradiction without maximizing the social response. Bjorn in established armor inside a fluorescent municipal checkpoint is extraordinary to the reader and merely the next procedural object for the building.

HOUSEHOLD BEHAVIOR: Carrie, Gunnar, Astrid and the Kin should not react as though Bjorn's armor is a joke either. They have arrived together; the comedy belongs to the collision between armor and process.

Spoiler ceiling: do not reveal the responsible-adult defect explicitly, individual testimony, Carrie's ownership of the old classification, Bjorn's decision to strike authority, the ruling, permanent-status outcome, or Astrid leaving afterward.

directionInline.text: Do not make this a fantasy battle poster. No swords, shields raised for combat, flames, judges as villains, gavels, courtroom theatrics, or triumphant victory imagery.
The image should make the reader think 'of course he wore armor' while every New Yorker in frame behaves as though the important question is whether it can go through the metal detector.
